newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo election latest casualty of bloody showdown.
newsitem.headline: Congo election latest casualty of bloody showdown.

text.p: Congo's July 27 presidential election became the latest casualty of a bloody power struggle in the capital Brazzaville on Tuesday after African leaders failed to broker a peace settlement.
President Pascal Lissouba, whose forces have been fighting militia loyal to former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, acknowledged that the elections could not take place on time as he had wished.
With mediators trying to relaunch their search for peace after the failure of Monday's peace talks in Gabon, Sassou Nguesso also said conditions were not ripe for elections.

In Brazzaville itself, supporters of the two men exchanged fire once again near the international airport as France continued to pull out its soldiers after evacuating more than 5,000 French and foreign nationals.

"The end of July will not be possible so long as people have arms...conditions do not permit it," Lissouba told Radio France International when asked if polling take place on time. "It's up to the constitutional council to fix another timetable."

Sassou Nguesso told the same radio station conditions were not in place for elections. He called for "a good transition period with transitional institutions to restore order and ask the international community to organise credible elections."

Fighting broke out in the city on June 5 after government troops surrounded the home of Sassou Nguesso as part of a crackdown on private militia and illegal possession of weapons in the runup to the election.
Lissouba won a 1992 presidential election called under a democratic transition launched by Sassou Nguesso and his single party. Sassou Nguesso became president in 1979.

An international mediation committee, led by Gabon's veteran president, Omar Bongo, said on Monday after a day of bilateral meetings with representatives of the warring parties and Congolese mediators that it had been unable to identify sufficient common ground for dialogue.
Gabonese officials told Reuters on Tuesday that efforts had begun to set the mediation initiative back on track.

Ex-colonial power France urged the mediators not to give up. "We very strongly encourage this committee to pursue any new initiative that could bring about a rapprochement between the Congolese parties," the Foreign Ministry in Paris said.
It added its voice to a call from the mediators for an immediate ceasefire. Sassou Nguesso and Lissouba urged their supporters on June 12 to cease fire.

U.N. and Organisation of African Unity special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, one of the mediators, expressed deep disappointment and blamed mutual suspicion. He highlighted "a lack of confidence in the conditions in which these elections should be held".
He said there was some cause for hope. "We want to work on the basis of these hopes," he said.
France has vowed to pull out its forces despite a request from Lissouba that it join a foreign buffer force. Lissouba has also called for deployment of an African peacekeeping force.
Health workers have been unable to piece together a reliable death toll for the Brazzaville clashes, which some sources say have killed hundreds, if not, several thousand people.
Political and ethnic clashes in Brazzaville killed at least 2,000 people following a disputed parliamentary election.
